title: The autonomy levels let an agent act, while the architecture says AI only suggests and a person approves
source: 08 AI and agents/Recovery Workbench AI and Agent Architecture v2.pptx (slides 2, 5, 6, 8, 9 and 11); 22 Microservice Realignment/Recovery Workbench Architecture v5 Text Extract v1.md (slides 16, 35, 41 and 43); 22 Microservice Realignment/Recovery Workbench Microservice Ownership Map v1.xlsx (sheet Workflows and activities)
section: AI and Agent Architecture v2 slides 2, 9 and 10; Architecture v5 slide 35 (AI under BOT AI risk rules)
description: Source slide 2 counts 10 automated, 13 advised and 2 person or partner sub-decisions, and source slide 9 defines five levels in which L2 acts inside a band, L3 acts across the decision and L4 acts and closes. Architecture v5 slide 35 states the rule as 'Suggests, never decides: a person approves' and 'human decision on material actions'. The two statements cannot both be read literally for a step at L2 to L4: either the agent acts and a person reviews a sample afterwards, or every decision waits for a person. No source says how a step at L2 to L4 is reconciled with the 'a person approves' line.
evidence: Source slide 2: '10 Automated | A rule, a model or an agent decides within policy and the result is logged'; 'L2 act in a band | The agent acts inside a narrow band; a person reviews a sample and the exceptions'; 'L4 act and close | The agent acts and closes; people monitor the measures'. Architecture v5 slide 35: 'Suggests, never decides: a person approves'; notes: 'human decision on material actions'.
proposed: Keep both: an advised decision (13 of the 25) keeps a person's approval whatever the level, and L2 to L4 add speed only inside a band the person set. Record the reconciliation in the AI decision governance document before a step is raised above L1.

title: The model endpoint of DL33 is 'a private endpoint in the SCB tenant'; Architecture v5 names INT-23 and no approval path
source: 08 AI and agents/Recovery Workbench AI and Agent Architecture v2.pptx (slides 2, 5, 6, 8, 9 and 11); 22 Microservice Realignment/Recovery Workbench Architecture v5 Text Extract v1.md (slides 16, 35, 41 and 43); 22 Microservice Realignment/Recovery Workbench Microservice Ownership Map v1.xlsx (sheet Services, P10)
section: AI and Agent Architecture v2 slides 5 and 11 (DL33); Architecture v5 slides 7 and 8
description: Source slide 5 places the model endpoint on 'the approved endpoint in the SCB tenant (DL33)' and slide 11 leaves DL33 open with the answer used until decided. Architecture v5 gives rwb-agent the Enterprise AI private endpoint and numbers it INT-23, but names no tenant, no hosting region, no interface version and no approval path for a new model version. Which endpoint a build points at, and who approves a change, is therefore not settled by a source.
evidence: Source slide 5: 'Model endpoint | On the approved endpoint in the SCB tenant (DL33)'; slide 11: 'DL33 | The model endpoint the agents call and where it is hosted | A private endpoint in the SCB tenant'. Architecture v5 slide 7: 'Enterprise AI private endpoint - rwb-agent'; slide 8 note: 'Outside: Enterprise AI private endpoint (INT-23) for rwb-agent'.
owner_role: Enterprise AI team and solution architect
proposed: Record INT-23 as the endpoint of the build until DL33 is closed, put the tenant, region and interface version in the rwb-agent interface contract, and name the model risk approval path as the only way a version changes.

title: Nine of the twelve agents have no service row that starts the run
source: 08 AI and agents/Recovery Workbench AI and Agent Architecture v2.pptx (slides 2, 5, 6, 8, 9 and 11); 22 Microservice Realignment/Recovery Workbench Architecture v5 Text Extract v1.md (slides 16, 35, 41 and 43); 22 Microservice Realignment/Recovery Workbench Microservice Ownership Map v1.xlsx (sheets Workflows and activities, Services)
section: AI and Agent Architecture v2 slide 6 (the agents); Architecture v5 slides 15, 16 and 18 (service contracts)
description: Source slide 6 lists twelve agents and their live and shadow epics but no caller. Architecture v5 names only three runs on a service contract: 'classify / extract run' on rwb-document (P5), 'screening agent run' on rwb-deviation (S8) and 'route agent' on rwb-valuation (S1). The settlement and restructure, valuation, pricing, guarantee claim, reconciliation, legal document, debt sale, write-off and tracing agents have no row in the Ownership Map and no contract that names who starts them, which leaves nine runs with no owner on the calling side.
evidence: Source slide 6: twelve rows, columns Agent, What it does, Live, Shadow. Architecture v5 slide 16: 'TMP Agent: child: classify / extract run' (P5 rwb-document); slide 15: 'TMP Agent: child: screening agent run' (S8 rwb-deviation); slide 18: 'TMP Agent: child: route agent' (S1 rwb-valuation). Ownership Map v1, sheet Workflows and activities: one row, AgentRunWorkflow, owner P10; no row per agent.
proposed: Name the calling service for each of the twelve agents in the Ownership Map (sheet Workflows and activities, one row per agent run) before wave 1, on the rule that the service that owns the stage decision starts the run.

title: The tool gateway is named by the source and given no owner
source: 08 AI and agents/Recovery Workbench AI and Agent Architecture v2.pptx (slides 2, 5, 6, 8, 9 and 11); 22 Microservice Realignment/Recovery Workbench Architecture v5 Text Extract v1.md (slides 16, 35, 41 and 43)
section: AI and Agent Architecture v2 slides 5 and 8; Architecture v5 slide 16
description: Source slide 5 says 'The orchestrator calls the agent through the tool gateway' and slide 8 says the gateway 'holds the permissions; the agent holds no credential'. Architecture v5 keeps one line, 'Tool gateway: read-only calls for the agent', in the rwb-agent contract, and lists P1 and P5 as the tools. No source says whether the gateway is a component inside rwb-agent, a shared edge component beside gateway-bff, or a capability of rwb-access (P4), so its deployment, its schema and its login are not decided.
evidence: Source slide 5: 'Tool gateway | The only way an agent reaches a system. No agent holds a credential'; slide 8: 'Tool gateway | The only way an agent reaches data or acts. The gateway holds the permissions; the agent holds no credential'. Architecture v5 slide 16: 'TMP AgentRunWorkflow: 60 s, then rule result - Tool gateway: read-only calls for the agent'; OUT: 'Source data: tool: read case facts - Document: tool: read extracted fields'.
proposed: Build the tool gateway inside rwb-agent: one outbound client that holds the workload identity, calls the owner's published REST contract, one hop and 2 s, and writes every call to the run row. Revisit if the platform edge later offers a shared agent gateway.

title: Who holds the AgentRunWorkflow handle and the parent-child link is not stated
source: 08 AI and agents/Recovery Workbench AI and Agent Architecture v2.pptx (slides 2, 5, 6, 8, 9 and 11); 22 Microservice Realignment/Recovery Workbench Architecture v5 Text Extract v1.md (slides 16, 35, 41 and 43); 22 Microservice Realignment/Recovery Workbench Temporal and Drools Design Text Extract v1.md (slide 13)
section: AI and Agent Architecture v2 slide 4 (agent child runs); Architecture v5 slides 15, 16, 18; Ownership Map sheet Workflows and activities
description: Architecture v5 gives AgentRunWorkflow to P10 on queue rwb-agent and, at the same time, gives the stage services an 'Agent: child' step inside their own workflow. The source does not say which workflow holds the child handle, which service computes the workflow ID, or what the two do when the child reports a fallback. The Ownership Map records one owner, P10, and no parent.
evidence: Architecture v5 slide 16: 'TMP AgentRunWorkflow: 60 s, then rule result' on queue rwb-agent (P10); slide 15 S8: 'TMP Agent: child: screening agent run'; slide 18 S1: 'TMP Agent: child: route agent'; Temporal and Drools design slide 13: the kit template 'Agent run with rule fallback'. Ownership Map v1: 'AgentRunWorkflow | P10'.
proposed: The calling workflow holds the child handle and passes caseId, step and run number; P10 owns the workflow type, its queue and its history. Write the rule into the workflow kit contract of RWB-PLT-E1071-CON.

title: The rule result used on a fallback is named for two agents only
source: 08 AI and agents/Recovery Workbench AI and Agent Architecture v2.pptx (slides 2, 5, 6, 8, 9 and 11); 22 Microservice Realignment/Recovery Workbench Architecture v5 Text Extract v1.md (slides 16, 35, 41 and 43); 22 Microservice Realignment/Recovery Workbench Temporal and Drools Design Text Extract v1.md (slides 12 and 13)
section: AI and Agent Architecture v2 slide 8 (fallback); Architecture v5 slide 16
description: The fallback rule is uniform in the source: if the agent does not answer within 60 seconds, 'the rule result is used and the fallback is recorded'. The Temporal and Drools design names R-UNI-32 for the route agent and the pricing agent only; it does not name the rule, the package or the version that supplies the result for the other ten agents. Without it a fallback cannot be shown to produce the same decision as the rule path.
evidence: Source slide 8: 'Fallback | If the agent does not answer within 60 seconds, the rule result is used and the fallback is recorded'. Temporal and Drools design slide 13: 'Agent run with rule fallback for the route agent and pricing agent (R-UNI-32)'; slide 14 table: 'AI agent slow: after 60 s the rule result is used (R-UNI-32)'.
proposed: Add one column to the agent policy row naming the rule package and version that supplies the fallback result for each of the twelve agents, and publish it with the rule registry of P7.

title: Who may change a prompt or a policy: the centre of excellence owns them, the admin endpoints are P10's
source: 08 AI and agents/Recovery Workbench AI and Agent Architecture v2.pptx (slides 2, 5, 6, 8, 9 and 11); 22 Microservice Realignment/Recovery Workbench Architecture v5 Text Extract v1.md (slides 16, 35, 41 and 43)
section: AI and Agent Architecture v2 slides 5, 8 and 10; Architecture v5 slide 16
description: Source slide 10 gives the centre of excellence ownership of prompts, policies and evaluation sets, and slide 8 requires versioned prompts and policies so a run can be reproduced. Architecture v5 gives rwb-agent 'GET/POST /agent-policies (admin)' and the rwb_agent tables. No source says who holds the admin role, whether a change needs maker-checker or a committee, or which roles P4 must grant, so the admin path exists without an authority behind it.
evidence: Source slide 10: 'Center of excellence | Owns prompts, policies and evaluation sets; proposes changes'; slide 8: 'Versioned prompts and policies | Each run records the prompt, policy, model and agent versions'. Architecture v5 slide 16: 'REST GET /agent-runs/{id} - GET/POST /agent-policies (admin)'.
owner_role: Center of excellence and P10 rwb-agent
proposed: Route /agent-policies writes through the rwb-access authorise contract (DP-08) with a maker-checker approval from P7, and record the approving role in the run row. Name the roles with the centre of excellence.

title: The 60 seconds: the whole run or the model call
source: 08 AI and agents/Recovery Workbench AI and Agent Architecture v2.pptx (slides 2, 5, 6, 8, 9 and 11); 22 Microservice Realignment/Recovery Workbench Architecture v5 Text Extract v1.md (slides 16, 35, 41 and 43); 22 Microservice Realignment/Recovery Workbench Temporal and Drools Design Text Extract v1.md (slide 14)
section: AI and Agent Architecture v2 slides 8 and 11 (DL11); Architecture v5 slide 16
description: The sources set a 60-second limit and do not say what it covers. Source slide 8 starts the clock at 'if the agent does not answer'; Architecture v5 writes 'AgentRunWorkflow: 60 s, then rule result', which reads as the whole workflow including the tool reads and the guardrail check; the NFR line reads 'AI agent: 60 s, then rule result'. A tool read of 2 s and a guardrail activity therefore sit inside or outside the same 60 s depending on the reading, which changes the budget the model gets.
evidence: Source slide 8: 'If the agent does not answer within 60 seconds, the rule result is used'; source slide 11: 'DL11 | Agent response target | 60 seconds, then the rule result is used'. Architecture v5 slide 16: 'TMP AgentRunWorkflow: 60 s, then rule result'; slide 39: 'AI agent runs | rwb-agent: 60 s, or the rule result is used'.
proposed: Set the 60 s on the whole AgentRunWorkflow: the timer starts when the workflow starts and a run that has not passed its guardrails at 60 s falls back. Publish the split (tool budget, model budget) in the agent policy row.

title: The model output is 'read from the daily load', but only rwb-source-data may read ACE data
source: 08 AI and agents/Recovery Workbench AI and Agent Architecture v2.pptx (slides 2, 5, 6, 8, 9 and 11); 22 Microservice Realignment/Recovery Workbench Architecture v5 Text Extract v1.md (slides 16, 35, 41 and 43)
section: AI and Agent Architecture v2 slide 7; Architecture v5 slides 7, 8 and 16
description: Source slide 7 says the models run in COLLINS and ACE and 'the Workbench reads their output from the daily load'. In the 19-service target the daily load lands in ACE and is read only through the 30 recovery.v_ace_* views by P1 (ADR-010, DP-05), and rwb-agent's contract lists P1 as a tool, not a view. The source does not say whether P10 sees the score as a tool read through P1's contract or as a field of its own, nor whether every score on slide 7 is exposed by a view.
evidence: Source slide 7: 'Models run in COLLINS and ACE under the bank model risk standard. The Workbench reads their output from the daily load.' Architecture v5 slide 16, P10 OUT: 'Source data: tool: read case facts'; slide 8 note: 'rwb-source-data reads ACE data through the 30 read-only recovery.v_ace_* views (ADR-010)'.
proposed: Read every score on slide 7 through P1's contract as a tool result, and confirm that each model inventory ID has a view column. Where one is missing, raise it with the ACE data owner rather than allowing a direct read.

title: The screen for a run and its gateway route have no owner row
source: 08 AI and agents/Recovery Workbench AI and Agent Architecture v2.pptx (slides 2, 5, 6, 8, 9 and 11); 22 Microservice Realignment/Recovery Workbench Architecture v5 Text Extract v1.md (slides 16, 35, 41 and 43); 22 Microservice Realignment/Recovery Workbench Microservice Ownership Map v1.xlsx (sheets Services, Endpoints)
section: AI and Agent Architecture v2 slide 8 (decision log and fallback shown to a person); Architecture v5 slide 16
description: Architecture v5 gives rwb-agent 'GET /agent-runs/{id}', which a person uses to see a proposal, a fallback and the versions behind it. Every screen call crosses gateway-bff with the Redis session and a composite route (DP-19), and the Ownership Map has no row for the edge, so neither the route nor the screen belongs to a service code in the sources.
evidence: Architecture v5 slide 16: 'REST GET /agent-runs/{id}'; slide 7: 'Recovery gateway-bff'; Rules R5.5 DP-19: 'Screen, ace-web | gateway-bff composite route | H RWB-PLT-N001-CON'. Ownership Map v1 sheet Services: 19 rows, none for gateway-bff.
proposed: Add the run screen to the RWB-PLT-N001-CON composite route story and keep the data owner P10. Raise the missing edge row once, in the platform work package, not per service.
